transcript:
Header:
Date: 2028-01-09
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Anita Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng), Evan Cole (Frostline Head of Platform), Priya Singh (Frostline Cloud Architect), Markus Vogel (Frostline CTO), Lena Park (Procurement)

Summary:
Short intro call to evaluate partnership for onramp of Frostline's SaaS model inference into Frostline's customer offering via cloud GPU partners. Discussed VPC/on-prem constraints, expected QPS and model families, routing and fallback options, and procurement/timing. Agreed next steps: share integration docs, schedule deep dive, exchange traffic profiles and benchmark template.

Topics:
- Integration patterns (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
- Network & compliance: VPC peering, private control plane, KMS
- Performance: latency SLOs, batch strategies, KV/ prefix caching
- Pricing and procurement signals for pilot/poC

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, account lead, with Diego and Anita on the call. Could you - Evan, maybe kick us off with a quick overview of what Frostline is trying to achieve?
[00:18] Evan Cole: Yeah hi, thanks Maya. So Frostline is, uh, an industrial SaaS for predictive quality on the manufacturing lines. We're building a new real-time inference layer for customers - want to offer lower latency, cheaper per-query pricing, and optionally host models in customer V P C s.
[00:34] Priya Singh: sorry, VPC not V P C, but yeah. We're exploring partners to help onramp GPU capacity and a runtime that can flex between hosted and private deployments.
[00:48] Diego Ramos: Got it. So high level, we usually see three patterns: hosted API for quick time to value, dedicated capacity for guaranteed throughput, and private / VPC onprem for regulated customers. Curious which of those you're leaning towards?
[01:05] Markus Vogel: We need a mix. The majority will be hosted initially, but our enterprise customers - about 15% - demand private VPC peering or even on-prem for air-gapped facilities.
[01:18] Lena Park: On the procurement side that's true, and we have to map procurement cycles - pilots to PO in about 6-9 months, ideally.
[01:27] Anita Patel: That's consistent. Quick question on models: what families are you evaluating? Are these LLaMA derivatives, Mistral, or larger models like GPT-style? That helps us plan quantization and kernel selection.
[01:41] Evan Cole: Mostly smaller Llama variants to start, a few 13B and 30B models for higher fidelity routes. Also some proprietary fine-tuned checkpoints we can't share publicly yet.
[01:51] Diego Ramos: Okay thanks. For those sizes we usually recommend 8-bit quant profiles for cost, but we need to validate perf for your latency SLOs. Could you share expected p99 latency targets and throughput?
[02:05] Priya Singh: We aim for p99 < 200ms for real-time inferencing on 256 token sequences, typical qps is about 120 steady with spikes to 600 during shifts.
[02:18] Maya Chen: Nice detail - that's really helpful. A few clarifying questions about networking - Priya you mentioned VPC peering, is that the preferred secure path or do you need a private control plane inside the customer's network too?
[02:33] Priya Singh: For some customers we need a customer-managed control plane or at least private endpoints. We also have KMS requirements - all keys stored via the customer's KMS and audit logs retained for three years.
[02:45] Diego Ramos: Understood. Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS via HSM integrations, and Private deployments can be delivered with a control plane inside their VPC. There might be a little friction for fully air-gapped on-prem, but we've done that with a packaging approach.
[03:01] Evan Cole: When you say packaging, do you mean a containerized onprem bundle? We have racks that are kind of locked down.
[03:08] Anita Patel: Yes some customers take our on-prem bundle; there's a separate ops checklist. We typically do a security review first - SOC2/ISO questions come up - and then we do an onsite or airgap packaging.
[03:20] Markus Vogel: Security review - yes. We'll probably need SOC 2 Type II, penetration test artifacts, and more. Do you have a standard security pack?
[03:29] Maya Chen: We do - I'll share the security dossier. It includes SOC2, data flow diagrams, penetration test summaries, and SAML SSO guidance.
[03:36] Lena Park: Also need to see contract SLAs and liability terms early for procurement to budget.
[03:41] Diego Ramos: On the perf side, a practical question: you mentioned 256 tokens p99 <200ms. That tends to be tight for 30B models on shared hosted infra without aggressive batching. For the spike of 600 qps you'd likely hit a contention issue. Two options: reserved Dedicated capacity or a mixed routing policy where critical traffic routes to Dedicated and best-effort to hosted.
[04:02] Priya Singh: Do you do automatic fallback between variants if capacity is hit?
[04:07] Diego Ramos: Yes - we can define routing policies by SLAs and cost buckets. If Dedicated is saturated we can fallback to a smaller model or a queued pathway with degraded SLOs. Also prefix/KV caching can reduce repeated tokens for chat-like requests.
[04:20] Evan Cole: Can KV cache help with prompt heavy workloads? Our prompts sometimes include long histories.
[04:24] Anita Patel: Absolutely. KV cache and prefix caching reduces repeated compute, and continuous batching helps throughput while maintaining low tail latencies. But it's workload dependent.
[04:34] Edward? [note: mis-transcribed] Speaker 6: mm hmm.
[04:38] Priya Singh: Another angle - encryption at rest for model weights. For proprietary weights we need assurances.
[04:43] Diego Ramos: We support encrypted storage and can run models in encrypted volumes; for Private deployments customers can manage keys with KMS.
[04:50] Maya Chen: On pricing, do you have target unit economics for the pilot? For example cost per 1k tokens or per-inference SLA tier?
[04:58] Lena Park: High level, procurement wants a per-call blended estimate and a peak pricing for dedicated blocks. We can share volumes to get a more accurate quote.
[05:08] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll send a benchmark template and cost model spreadsheet - it'll let you plug in your traffic and model mixes to see estimated unit costs.
[05:16] Evan Cole: Perfect. A couple of deep questions for Diego: what's the onboarding footprint for a private control plane? How long to get an initial pilot running?
[05:26] Diego Ramos: For a Private deployment in a VPC it's typically 4-6 weeks for the initial install and security assessment, assuming network prerequisites are met. Hosted pilot can be live in days with sample integration. Dedicated reserved capacity provisioning depends on GPU availability but we can scope an initial capacity as a pilot in 2-3 weeks.
[05:43] Priya Singh: If we want to do on-prem air-gapped, what's the checklist?
[05:47] Anita Patel: We'll need a hardware spec (GPUs, networking), offline package for the control plane, standard install runbook, and an ops contact. There are also licensing terms we share.
[05:58] Evan Cole: Good. Let's talk success criteria – what would make a pilot successful?
[06:02] Maya Chen: From Redwood's perspective success would be: (1) validated latency/throughput at pilot scale, (2) integration of KMS and audit log flow, (3) a jointly agreed cost model for production, and (4) security sign-off.
[06:13] Markus Vogel: That matches ours - add a readiness for canary rollouts and a rollback plan.
[06:19] Diego Ramos: On rollouts, we support canary and A/B with automatic fallback to previous model or smaller variant. We also have tracing hooks to compare outputs across variants to check for regressions.
[06:32] Priya Singh: Very useful. On the legal side - any non-standard terms for model weights? We use customer-supplied proprietary fine-tunes; are there restrictions on residency or retention?
[06:44] Maya Chen: Customers can choose residency options in Private or Dedicated. Hosted has retention controls and enterprise retention tiers. For proprietary weights, Private is the safest. We'll add that into the security/ops doc I share.
[06:54] Evan Cole: Great. Procurement question - if we kick off a pilot in March, is that a realistic time to have pilot results by May?
[07:02] Lena Park: That timeline aligns; procurement could sign pilot SOW in February if security and budgets align.
[07:08] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Back to technical - Diego, can you run a short primer on how our runtime manages batching and latency tradeoffs?
[07:17] Diego Ramos: Sure. Our runtime uses continuous batching - it dynamically accumulates requests up to a latency threshold then dispatches. For low-latency p99 SLOs we tune the threshold lower and reduce batch sizes, which increases cost. We also do proactive KV caching for repeated prefixes and offer quantization profiles to reduce GPU memory and increase throughput. There's a compile-time kernel selector to pick the best kernels for sequence length distributions.
[07:44] Priya Singh: The kernel selector - is that automatic or do you need help from us to profile sequences?
[07:49] Diego Ramos: It's automatic but it benefits from sample traffic profiles - if you share a representative week of requests we can pre-tune.
[07:56] Evan Cole: We'll share that. Any thought on cost for 600 qps spike handling?
[08:01] Anita Patel: It depends on model sizes and batching. The spreadsheet will give a rough estimate; for spikes often a mix of reserved baseline plus burst to hosted is most cost-effective.
[08:12] Markus Vogel: One more: SLA & incident response. How does Redwood engage on incidents?
[08:18] Maya Chen: Our enterprise SLAs come with 24x7 support for production incidents, an on-call rotation, and defined RTO/RPO per contract. We'll include SLA examples in the follow-up.
[08:28] Evan Cole: Cool. I think we have enough to move forward to the technical deep dive.
[08:32] Maya Chen: Recap then - Redwood to share security pack, partner integration guide, terraform samples, benchmark template and cost model spreadsheet. Frostline will send traffic profiles and list of model weights plus internal timeline. We'll schedule a 90-min deep dive next week to map VPC and onprem constraints.
[08:50] Lena Park: Procurement will need an initial SOW and estimated costs to present to finance; can you include that in the follow-up?
[08:55] Maya Chen: Yes we'll include an outline SOW and estimated pricing range.
[09:00] Markus Vogel: Any blockers from Redwood side we should know about?
[09:03] Diego Ramos: Nothing immediate. We'll want the traffic profile and network diagrams to get started.
[09:10] Priya Singh: We'll get those by Friday.
[09:12] Evan Cole: Thanks all.
[09:14] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with links and next steps.

Post-call notes:
- Shared links: security dossier (link placeholder), partner getting-started repo, benchmark spreadsheet (we noted attachments will be sent).
